overview: Anguthimri is a western Cape York language label under which scholars have described Mpakwithi. This page follows documented Mpakwithi language work and the wider Mapoon community’s experiences. The mission brought together several peoples, so its residents and histories cannot all be treated as one undifferentiated group.

periods.title: Life under the Mapoon mission
periods.summary: A mission established on Tjungundji Country brought together people from different communities. Schooling, work and residence were shaped by church and government authority.

periods.title: Removal and resistance
periods.summary: Authorities forced remaining residents from Mapoon and destroyed homes. Jean Jimmy carried the campaign against removal into a national Indigenous rights forum in 1964.

periods.title: Return and community organization
periods.summary: Families began returning to Old Mapoon in 1974. Marpuna Aboriginal Corporation, established in 1984, helped rebuild community facilities and support return.

periods.title: Remembered songs support renewal
periods.summary: The language program describes hymns remembered by the Kennedy sisters as a starting point for renewed Mpakwithi learning from 2018.

periods.title: Family memory becomes a film
periods.summary: A Mpakwithi song by Susan Kennedy and artwork drawn from community memories were combined in a short film about her mother.

periods.title: Voices of Old Mapoon reaches new audiences
periods.summary: A community launch in 2023 was followed by festival recognition reported in 2024. The film combines recollection, music, painting and animation.

items.text: Pama Language Centre cites Terry Crowley’s study of Mpakwithi as a dialect of Anguthimri. Its teaching notes explain that complex word-building patterns were made more regular for adults learning the language, while distinctive sounds were retained. This is a described revival strategy, not evidence that earlier speakers used a simplified grammar.

Crowley’s archived Mpakwithi materials include elicitation notes on kinship, possession, adjectives and grammatical cases. The finding aid warns that early notes contain inconsistencies and points to checked published forms. Such records preserve evidence for research and renewal, but an archival label alone cannot establish a reliable translation.

Cape York Partnership’s 2023 report traces the revival initiative to three hymns remembered by the Kennedy sisters, which their grandfather had taught them. The account shows how family memory supplied material for learning after a long interruption in everyday language use. It does not demonstrate uninterrupted fluency across every generation.

Mapoon mission was founded in 1891 on Tjungundji land. Authorities later sent children and adults from other places there. After the destruction and removal of the 1960s, families returned to Old Mapoon from 1974. The rebuilt community and New Mapoon are distinct places, connected by this history of displacement.

Jean Jimmy’s biography describes childhood in the mission dormitory, English-only lessons, sewing and domestic training. Later, she worked in domestic service while her husband worked at sea. She also learned bush-food and medicinal knowledge from her mother. Her particular life records both institutional restrictions and family teaching, rather than a universal Mapoon childhood.

Federal correspondence preserved as National Archives file A884, A2863 shows that promised direct pension payments did not end state control. Officials still managed bank accounts, scrutinized spending and supervised the New Mapoon store. These documents make financial restrictions visible in the practical matters of buying food and receiving income.

The State Library describes a set of pre-closure slides showing Mapoon infrastructure that church and government authorities had judged inadequate. Their archival context matters: images made or retained by administrators can reveal buildings while also reflecting the institutions seeking closure. The catalog does not by itself establish what each resident thought of those homes.

Jean Jimmy attended the 1964 national FCAATSI conference to explain residents’ efforts at self-sufficiency and oppose their treatment. She later chaired community councils. Her political work demonstrates that residents challenged removal and government control; their story was not simply a sequence of official decisions made elsewhere.

At a community-requested gathering in Bamaga, participants developed work connecting language with memories of Old Mapoon. Susan Kennedy composed and sang in Mpakwithi about her mother. The 2021 project account identifies family paintings and illustrations as source material for an animated short, giving named community creators a central role in telling the history.

Voices of Old Mapoon, directed by Johnny Mark and Karin Calley, brings remembered childhood and forced removal together through speech, singing, painting and animation. The producing organization reported its New Mapoon launch in 2023 and selection as a Canberra Short Film Festival finalist in 2024. Selection is not the same as winning an award.

The 2021 short used memories and images contributed by people who had experienced removal as children. Combining their work with a newly composed song created a public historical account rooted in family experience. The project report documents its production; it does not establish that everyone remembered the events identically or evaluate clinical outcomes.

ending.text: The end of fluent everyday transmission in some families did not end their people or cultural identity. Mpakwithi community members continue language and artistic work while remembering removal from Old Mapoon. The map’s 1815 endpoint is a limit of its coverage, not a date of disappearance.
